newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU Commission to referee wheat licence skirmish.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission to referee wheat licence skirmish.

text.p: European Union grain exporters awaited weekly export tender results on Thursday uncertain how the European Commission would react to a wide range of subsidy bids, as the July/June export campaign enters its last straight.

The market is by now reasonably well supplied with export licences overall, traders said. But it remains split down the middle between exporters said to be long of licences and those racing against the clock to cover urgent business.
Having apparently failed to resolve the problem through secondary licence trading, several say they are now looking to Brussels to settle a market tussle dating back several weeks.
But with the world market also lacking clear direction, the task facing the Brussels-based Commission did not look easy.
"With a spread of more than 10 Ecus per tonne between the lowest and highest (refund bids) in France, it's clear Brussels will have a problem making a decision today," one trader said.
In France traders bid for 290,500 tonnes of soft wheat at refunds between 4.74 and 14.99 Ecus per tonne.
The tonnage sought through France is lower than in previous weeks. But the gap between bids remains around the same, even if fewer were packed in at the lowest subsidy levels this week.
Traders said there were two main scenarios for the tender.

Some exporters believed the Commission would go as high as 9.45 Ecus per tonne -- a level which, according to an unofficial breakdown of French bids, would allow some 185,000 tonnes of wheat to be released for export at a fob price near $165/tonne.
Others disagreed, saying Brussels would more likely place the cut-off lower in order to save money on export subsidies.

Traders said the top refund under this scenario might be closer to six Ecus, allowing the EU to save three Ecus compared to the last award two weeks ago (without allowing for the loss of a monthly increment for prompt shipments since last time).
Earlier this week, refunds were being offered between traders on the market at between four and five Ecus.
That sort of refund would point to an export price at a hefty $170 per tonne, fob France, traders said.
Second-guessing the Commission's decision was complicated this week by the comparatively low volume of bids in France, leading some traders to suspect heavy unseen bidding elsewhere.
France is among the few EU member states to publish the tonnage sought as well as the range of bids each week.
One thing, however, was certain, traders said.
Exporters still short of licences had little margin for manoeuvre and would be at the market's mercy if the Commission did not come to their aid.
The situation would become particularly difficult to manage if the EU decided to end export licence awards for the current season before the end of this month, traders said.
According to one EU official, the trade block has potential scope to issue another 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes in licences before the end of the campaign, should it decide to do so.
